Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

Investigation PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography. Objectives: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

Investigation PSI-106 (SLICE): Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment. Objectives: Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames. Approach: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. literature.title: Spacecraft Fire Safety: Saffire I–VI Large-Scale Cygnus Flight Experiments & SoFIE Exploration Atmospheres
literature.authors: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff, Paul V. Ferkul, Justin T. Niehaus
literature.platform: Northrop Grumman Cygnus Spacecraft & ISS CIR (SoFIE)
literature.excerpt: Saffire I–VI conducted full-scale (up to 0.4 m x 1.0 m) cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) and ribbed/flat PMMA burns inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicles after ISS departure across normoxic (21% O2, 101.3 kPa) and Artemis Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA: 34% O2 at 56.5 kPa / 8.2 psia). Findings demonstrate that in finite cabin volumes, large fires couple strongly with vehicle pressure rise and oxygen depletion, while elevated O2 mole fraction (34% O2) significantly increases flame spread rate and CO/soot yields despite reduced total cabin pressure. SoFIE (MIST, GEL, SMuRF) extends these measurements inside the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack.

literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Plugs-Out Pad Test Cabin Fire Investigation & High-O2 Flammability Lessons
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Apollo 204 Review Board
literature.excerpt: On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire in Apollo 1 (CM-012) during a pre-launch plugs-out test in a 100% O2, 16.7 psia (115 kPa) atmosphere resulted in the loss of the three-person crew. Pure oxygen at elevated partial pressure drastically lowered the ignition energy and accelerated flame propagation across exposed Nylon netting, Velcro hooks, and polyurethane foam. Apollo 1 established strict material flammability controls (NHB 8060.1 / NASA-STD-6001), restricted exposed Velcro/polymer fuel paths, and motivated dual-gas N2/O2 cabin atmospheres.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

Investigation PSI-68 (FLEX-2): Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2. Objectives: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
  1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
  2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
  3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
  4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.

The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

Investigation PSI-68 (FLEX-2): Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2. Objectives: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
  1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
  2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
  3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
  4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
  5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
  6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.     1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
    2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
    3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
    4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion. Approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Plugs-Out Pad Test Cabin Fire Investigation & High-O2 Flammability Lessons
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Apollo 204 Review Board
literature.excerpt: On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire in Apollo 1 (CM-012) during a pre-launch plugs-out test in a 100% O2, 16.7 psia (115 kPa) atmosphere resulted in the loss of the three-person crew. Pure oxygen at elevated partial pressure drastically lowered the ignition energy and accelerated flame propagation across exposed Nylon netting, Velcro hooks, and polyurethane foam. Apollo 1 established strict material flammability controls (NHB 8060.1 / NASA-STD-6001), restricted exposed Velcro/polymer fuel paths, and motivated dual-gas N2/O2 cabin atmospheres.

gravity material flammability screening test. Approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

Investigation PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. Objectives: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. Hypothesis: The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.platform: Space Shuttle & ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (SAME / DAFT)
literature.excerpt: In microgravity, the absence of buoyant plumes causes pyrolysis and smoldering smoke aerosols (from Kapton, Teflon, Silicone, Cellulose, and Lamp Wick tested in SAME PSI-102 and SAME-R PSI-101) to remain in the flame/heater zone longer, growing into larger agglomerated particles (0.2–1.5 micrometers count median diameter) than in 1g. ISS photoelectric laser-scattering detectors are tuned differently from shuttle ionization detectors; understanding particle size distributions and dust discrimination (DAFT PSI-47) prevents nuisance alarms while ensuring rapid detection of pre-flaming pyrolysis.

literature.title: Apollo 13 Service Module Oxygen Tank No. 2 PTFE Insulation Ignition & Cryogenic O2 Hazard
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Cortright Review Board
literature.excerpt: During Apollo 13 in April 1970, damaged 28V/65V thermostatic switches inside supercritical Oxygen Tank No. 2 overheated (>500 °C during pre-flight detanking) and ignited fluoropolymer (PTFE / Teflon) wire insulation in high-pressure pure oxygen upon fan stirring. Even materials classified as non-flammable in normal air (PTFE) undergo rapid exothermic combustion in high-pressure pure O2 without buoyant heat dissipation.

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.excerpt:
Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.authors: Sandra L. Paul Funiaki James Olson Ferkul Takahashi T'ien
literature.keywords: Flame Spread     Fire suppression system     Damkohler number     Boundary layer     Fire safety     Forced Flow Flame     Kinetic regime
literature.excerpt:
Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

Investigation PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I): Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I. Objectives: The objectives of this investigation were to:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal
gravity material flammability screening test. Approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

literature.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Plugs-Out Pad Test Cabin Fire Investigation & High-O2 Flammability Lessons
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Apollo 204 Review Board
literature.excerpt: On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire in Apollo 1 (CM-012) during a pre-launch plugs-out test in a 100% O2, 16.7 psia (115 kPa) atmosphere resulted in the loss of the three-person crew. Pure oxygen at elevated partial pressure drastically lowered the ignition energy and accelerated flame propagation across exposed Nylon netting, Velcro hooks, and polyurethane foam. Apollo 1 established strict material flammability controls (NHB 8060.1 / NASA-STD-6001), restricted exposed Velcro/polymer fuel paths, and motivated dual-gas N2/O2 cabin atmospheres.

literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Plugs-Out Pad Test Cabin Fire Investigation & High-O2 Flammability Lessons
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Apollo 204 Review Board
literature.excerpt: On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire in Apollo 1 (CM-012) during a pre-launch plugs-out test in a 100% O2, 16.7 psia (115 kPa) atmosphere resulted in the loss of the three-person crew. Pure oxygen at elevated partial pressure drastically lowered the ignition energy and accelerated flame propagation across exposed Nylon netting, Velcro hooks, and polyurethane foam. Apollo 1 established strict material flammability controls (NHB 8060.1 / NASA-STD-6001), restricted exposed Velcro/polymer fuel paths, and motivated dual-gas N2/O2 cabin atmospheres.

literature.title: Spacecraft Smoke Detection & Aerosol Signatures in Microgravity (SAME / DAFT / Shuttle Spinoff)
literature.authors: David L. Urban, Marit E. Meyer, Gary A. Ruff, Paul D. Mudgett
literature.platform: Space Shuttle & ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (SAME / DAFT)
literature.excerpt: In microgravity, the absence of buoyant plumes causes pyrolysis and smoldering smoke aerosols (from Kapton, Teflon, Silicone, Cellulose, and Lamp Wick tested in SAME PSI-102 and SAME-R PSI-101) to remain in the flame/heater zone longer, growing into larger agglomerated particles (0.2–1.5 micrometers count median diameter) than in 1g. ISS photoelectric laser-scattering detectors are tuned differently from shuttle ionization detectors; understanding particle size distributions and dust discrimination (DAFT PSI-47) prevents nuisance alarms while ensuring rapid detection of pre-flaming pyrolysis.

literature.title: Spacecraft Fire Safety: Saffire I–VI Large-Scale Cygnus Flight Experiments & SoFIE Exploration Atmospheres
literature.authors: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff, Paul V. Ferkul, Justin T. Niehaus
literature.platform: Northrop Grumman Cygnus Spacecraft & ISS CIR (SoFIE)
literature.excerpt: Saffire I–VI conducted full-scale (up to 0.4 m x 1.0 m) cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) and ribbed/flat PMMA burns inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicles after ISS departure across normoxic (21% O2, 101.3 kPa) and Artemis Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA: 34% O2 at 56.5 kPa / 8.2 psia). Findings demonstrate that in finite cabin volumes, large fires couple strongly with vehicle pressure rise and oxygen depletion, while elevated O2 mole fraction (34% O2) significantly increases flame spread rate and CO/soot yields despite reduced total cabin pressure. SoFIE (MIST, GEL, SMuRF) extends these measurements inside the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack.

literature.authors: Sandra L. Paul Funiaki James Olson Ferkul Takahashi T'ien
literature.keywords: Flame Spread     Fire suppression system     Damkohler number     Boundary layer     Fire safety     Forced Flow Flame     Kinetic regime
literature.excerpt:
Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

Objectives: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test. Approach: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.authors: Alice Derek Dennis Chien Dunn-Rankin Stocker

Investigation PSI-22 (ACME E-FIELD Flames): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames. Objectives: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames. Approach: The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. Investigation PSI-25 (BASS-II): Burning and Suppression of Solids - II. Objectives: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
Objectives Include:
  1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
  2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.

The primary variables include:

Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

Objectives: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

literature.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Plugs-Out Pad Test Cabin Fire Investigation & High-O2 Flammability Lessons
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Apollo 204 Review Board
literature.excerpt: On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire in Apollo 1 (CM-012) during a pre-launch plugs-out test in a 100% O2, 16.7 psia (115 kPa) atmosphere resulted in the loss of the three-person crew. Pure oxygen at elevated partial pressure drastically lowered the ignition energy and accelerated flame propagation across exposed Nylon netting, Velcro hooks, and polyurethane foam. Apollo 1 established strict material flammability controls (NHB 8060.1 / NASA-STD-6001), restricted exposed Velcro/polymer fuel paths, and motivated dual-gas N2/O2 cabin atmospheres.

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

Objectives: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. Approach: The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

Investigation PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. Objectives: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).

5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

Objectives: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames. Investigation PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. Objectives: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions.   4. Inverse cool diffusion flames

literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

Investigation PSI-69 (FLEX): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. Approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .

literature.authors: Sandra L. Paul Funiaki James Olson Ferkul Takahashi T'ien
literature.keywords: Flame Spread     Fire suppression system     Damkohler number     Boundary layer     Fire safety     Forced Flow Flame     Kinetic regime
literature.excerpt:
Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

literature.title: Low-Velocity Microgravity Flame Spread and Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) vs. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

literature.title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) Plugs-Out Pad Test Cabin Fire Investigation & High-O2 Flammability Lessons
literature.authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance (OSMA) / Apollo 204 Review Board
literature.excerpt: On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire in Apollo 1 (CM-012) during a pre-launch plugs-out test in a 100% O2, 16.7 psia (115 kPa) atmosphere resulted in the loss of the three-person crew. Pure oxygen at elevated partial pressure drastically lowered the ignition energy and accelerated flame propagation across exposed Nylon netting, Velcro hooks, and polyurethane foam. Apollo 1 established strict material flammability controls (NHB 8060.1 / NASA-STD-6001), restricted exposed Velcro/polymer fuel paths, and motivated dual-gas N2/O2 cabin atmospheres.

literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.

literature.excerpt: Investigation PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis. Objectives: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects. Approach: OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. literature.title: Spacecraft Fire Safety: Saffire I–VI Large-Scale Cygnus Flight Experiments & SoFIE Exploration Atmospheres
literature.authors: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff, Paul V. Ferkul, Justin T. Niehaus
literature.platform: Northrop Grumman Cygnus Spacecraft & ISS CIR (SoFIE)
literature.excerpt: Saffire I–VI conducted full-scale (up to 0.4 m x 1.0 m) cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) and ribbed/flat PMMA burns inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicles after ISS departure across normoxic (21% O2, 101.3 kPa) and Artemis Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA: 34% O2 at 56.5 kPa / 8.2 psia). Findings demonstrate that in finite cabin volumes, large fires couple strongly with vehicle pressure rise and oxygen depletion, while elevated O2 mole fraction (34% O2) significantly increases flame spread rate and CO/soot yields despite reduced total cabin pressure. SoFIE (MIST, GEL, SMuRF) extends these measurements inside the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack.

literature.excerpt:
Investigation PSI-26 (BASS): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Investigation PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography. Objectives: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.

literature.authors: Sandra L. Olson, Fletcher J. Miller, Indrek S. Wichman, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & GRC Drop Tower
literature.excerpt: Standard spacecraft material qualification relies on terrestrial 1g upward flame spread testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), where buoyant flow (~30–50 cm/s) convectively cools the flame zone. In microgravity at low spacecraft HVAC velocities (1.5–15 cm/s), convective heat loss drops while oxygen transport to the pyrolysis front remains active. Consequently, the 0g Minimum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) boundary is 2.5% to 4.0% O2 lower than in 1g, meaning materials certified as self-extinguishing on Earth (e.g., thin PMMA, Nomex, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL) can sustain flame spread in orbit unless ventilation fans are shut off (<1.0 cm/s diffusive starvation).

Investigation PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. Objectives: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples. Hypothesis: The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames

literature.title: A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (NASA NP-2015-03-015-JSC)
literature.authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Paul V. Ferkul
literature.excerpt: In microgravity (0g), buoyant natural convection vanishes (~10^-6 g on the ISS), transforming teardrop flames into spherical diffusion flames governed by molecular diffusion, radiative heat loss, and low-velocity forced ventilation (1–25 cm/s). Droplet combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) revealed two-stage burning: high-temperature hot-flame radiative extinction followed by sustained low-temperature (~600–750 K) cool flames stabilized by alkylperoxy (RO2) chemistry in n-heptane and n-decane. Solid fuel tests in BASS and BASS-II proved that gentle cabin ventilation supplies fresh oxidizer without buoyant cooling, allowing materials to burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth.
